    Template

    Design token starter kit

    A small JSON token structure and a decision checklist for consistent interface patterns.

    What is inside

    A small JSON token structure and a decision checklist for consistent interface patterns. It is written to be used, not read once: every page is a step you can run this week with your own work.

    • The short version, on one page
    • The full checklist with examples
    • A blank version to fill in

    Who it is for

    Designers, engineers and instructors who want a repeatable process rather than another opinion.

    A shared language for interface decisions

    A small token set. A consistent starting point.

    An actual JSON starter with semantic colours, spacing and a control radius. Adapt the values, check contrast and connect it to your own build tools.

    {
  "color": {
    "ink": {
      "$type": "color",
      "$value": "#012A5D",
      "$description": "Readable text on a light surface"
    },
    "surface": {
      "$type": "color",
      "$value": "#FFFFFF"
    },
    "accent": {
      "$type": "color",
      "$value": "#C8F560",
      "$description": "Pair with dark text"
    }
  },
  "space": {
    "1": {
      "$type": "dimension",
      "$value": {
        "value": 4,
        "unit": "px"
      }
    },
    "2": {
      "$type": "dimension",
      "$value": {
        "value": 8,
        "unit": "px"
      }
    },
    "3": {
      "$type": "dimension",
      "$value": {
        "value": 12,
        "unit": "px"
      }
    },
    "4": {
      "$type": "dimension",
      "$value": {
        "value": 16,
        "unit": "px"
      }
    }
  },
  "radius": {
    "control": {
      "$type": "dimension",
      "$value": {
        "value": 12,
        "unit": "px"
      }
    }
  }
}

    An accessible, readable alternative

    The workbook, right here.

    The same text as the downloadable PDF, available without a PDF reader.

    01 / Understand the task

    A small JSON token structure and a decision checklist for consistent interface patterns.

    Give repeated interface decisions a shared name, a value and a reason for existing.

    Choose one small, real example to work on. A focused attempt gives you better evidence than a general impression.

    Your example: ____________________________________________________________

    Your audience: ___________________________________________________________

    Your intended outcome: ___________________________________________________

    One constraint: __________________________________________________________

    02 / Put a method to work

    1. Inventory three repeated decisions: ink colour, spacing and corner radius.

    2. Use semantic names such as color.ink rather than blue-1.

    3. Record a value, type and short purpose for each token.

    4. Keep component aliases separate from the underlying palette.

    5. Test the values in a button, a field and a readable paragraph.

    6. Document how a token changes across light and dark surfaces.

    Working notes: __________________________________________________________

    _________________________________________________________________________

    03 / A worked practice scenario

    Example token: color.ink = #012A5D, used for readable text on light surfaces.

    Example spacing scale: space.1 = 4px, space.2 = 8px, space.3 = 12px, space.4 = 16px.

    The resource page includes an actual downloadable JSON starter. It is a sample structure, not a production build system.

    Apply the method to your own example. What changes?

    Your first attempt: _______________________________________________________

    Your revision: ___________________________________________________________

    04 / Reflect and keep going

    Can a teammate choose the right value from its purpose rather than its appearance?

    What is clearer after using this workbook?

    _________________________________________________________________________

    What evidence supports that conclusion?

    _________________________________________________________________________

    What is the smallest useful next step?

    _________________________________________________________________________

    Feedback prompt: "I noticed ____. That helped / made it harder to ____. One thing to try is ____."

    You may adapt this original sample workbook for personal learning and classroom demonstrations.
